title: Haudenosaunee
wiki_lead:
The Haudenosaunee Confederacy ( HOH-din-oh-SHOH-nee; lit. 'those who build the longhouse'), also known as the Iroquois, is a confederacy of Iroquoian Indigenous peoples in northeast North America. They have also been called the Six Nations (Five Nations before 1722). The Haudenosaunee originally comprised (from east to west) the Mohawk, Oneida, Onondaga, Cayuga, and Seneca peoples. After 1722, the Iroquoian-speaking Tuscarora migrated from the southeast and were accepted into the Confederacy.
Haudenosaunee oral history describes the formation of the Confederacy by the Great Peacemaker, Hiawatha, and Jigonhsasee under a constitution known as the Great Law of Peace, likely between 1142 and 1660, although there is little agreement on the date. Contact with Europeans began with the arrival of Dutch colonists to North America, which the Haudenosaunee describe as the origin of the Two Row Wampum Treaty. The acquisition of muskets through the fur trade led to a rapid expansion in Haudenosaunee strength during the Beaver Wars, during which time they dispersed or assimilated most neighboring tribes. At its peak around 1700, Haudenosaunee power extended from what is today New York State, north into present-day Ontario and Quebec along the lower Great Lakes–upper St. Lawrence, and south on both sides of the Allegheny Mountains into present-day Virginia, Kentucky, and the Ohio Valley.
For nearly 200 years, the Haudenosaunee were a central player in North American geopolitics, often holding the balance of power between the French and British colonies. The Haudenosaunee eventually aligned with the British under the Covenant Chain, backing the British during the French and Indian War and securing protection from westward colonial expansion through the Royal Proclamation of 1763. During the American Revolution, Haudenosaunee unity collapsed, with the Oneida and Tuscarora fighting alongside the Patriots and the other nations of the Confederacy allying with the British. In the wake of American independence and the devastating Sullivan Expedition, many Haudenosaunee fled to British Canada, establishing the Six Nations of the Grand River reserve. Haudenosaunee territory in the United States was further reduced by a series of land cessions and sales, and political unity divided between numerous Tribal and First Nation governments. Nonetheless, the Haudenosaunee reestablished the Grand Council of the Confederacy after the Revolution and continue to consider themselves sovereign and independent. The Haudenosaunee issue their own passports and attempted to join the League of Nations in 1923.
In 2010, more than 45,000 enrolled Six Nations people lived in Canada, and over 81,000 in the United States. They retain sovereignty over seven reserves in Canada and eleven reservations in the United States, divided between seventeen First Nations and nine Tribal nations.

Names

The autonym Haudenosaunee means "people of the longhouse", in reference to the metaphorical longhouse formed by the five original nations of the League. This "longhouse" stretched from the Mohawk Nation in the east to the Seneca Nation in the west, the former being designated the "Keepers of the Eastern Door" and the latter the "Keepers of the Western Door". Iroquois, the traditional exonym for the Haudenosaunee, is of obscure and debated origin, first appearing in the 1603 writings of the French explorer Samuel de Champlain. The descriptive term "Five Nations" (or, after 1722, "Six Nations") is also used, particularly in historical documents. A less common, older autonym for the people of the League is Ongweh’onweh, meaning "original people". The Haudenosaunee country has been called Iroquoia and Haudenosauneega in English, and Iroquoisie in French.
